lesson.title: The Electrons That Do All the Chemistry
lesson.summary: Valence electrons are the electrons in an atom's outermost shell, the ones available for bonding and reacting, and counting them directly from an electron configuration explains why elements in the same group behave alike.
lesson.body:
Not every electron in an atom matters equally for chemistry. Electrons buried in inner, completely filled shells sit close to the nucleus, tightly bound and largely shielded from other atoms. The electrons that actually participate in forming bonds, gaining or losing charge, and reacting with other substances are the ones in the outermost occupied shell, the shell with the highest principal quantum number n. Chemists call these valence electrons, and identifying them is really just a matter of reading an electron configuration you already know how to write and picking out the electrons with the largest n value.

Chlorine makes a clean worked example. Chlorine, atomic number 17, has the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5 (2+2+6+2+5 = 17, confirming the electron count). The highest shell present is n = 3, so the valence electrons are the ones in 3s and 3p: 2 electrons in 3s plus 5 electrons in 3p gives 7 valence electrons total. The ten electrons in 1s, 2s, and 2p are not counted as valence, because they belong to the completed, lower n = 1 and n = 2 shells.

This connects directly to how the periodic table itself, the table of elements you have already studied, is organized. For main group elements, the group number lines up with the valence electron count in a very direct way: group 1 elements (like sodium and potassium) have 1 valence electron, group 2 elements have 2, and groups 13 through 18 have 3 through 8 valence electrons respectively. Chlorine sits in group 17, the halogens, and indeed has 7 valence electrons, matching the pattern exactly. This is not a coincidence chemists memorized after the fact; the periodic table's column structure was built around exactly this kind of recurring valence pattern, which is why elements in the same column share such similar chemical behavior.

Valence electron count explains reactivity directly. Elements with nearly full or nearly empty valence shells tend to react vigorously, because gaining or losing just one or two electrons lets them reach a stable, filled outer shell resembling the nearest noble gas. Chlorine, with 7 valence electrons, needs only one more electron to reach a full octet of 8, which is exactly why chlorine so readily grabs an electron from a metal like sodium to form the ionic compound sodium chloride, ordinary table salt. Sodium, by contrast, has only 1 valence electron (configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1) and loses it easily to reach the same stable, noble gas like electron count as neon.

Valence electrons are also the electrons drawn in Lewis dot structures and the electrons whose interactions determine bond type, molecular shape, and much of a compound's reactivity. Once you can reliably pick valence electrons out of any electron configuration, the next natural step is asking what is left over, the electrons that are not valence, which is exactly the idea of core electrons covered next.
